https://www.delfi.lt/en/politics/vatican.text: Delfi EN Delfi Politics 2026.08.13 18:29 Vatican informed about pedophilia scandal – media Translated by Karolis Broga Source: Elta EN Vatican informed about pedophilia scandal – media PHOTO: ELTA / Marius Morkevičius Follow Delfi on Google The Vatican is aware about the pedophilia scandal in Lithuania after prosecutors transferred to court criminal cases involving two priests suspected of sexual crimes against minors and possession of pornography depicting children. The Apostolic Nunciature confirmed to the news website 15min.lt that the Holy See has been informed about the two cases. The Vatican has expressed solidarity with the families of the victims. The Apostolic Nunciature expressed its trust in the investigations of competent state institutions and the work done by the Archdiocese of Vilnius, and is awaiting findings in their proceedings, 15min reported Thursday. The Vatican stated that it had received information from the Archdiocese of Vilnius about the investigation, but did not specify the exact date. Moreover, the Vatican said it has been following the case with great concern, stressing that there is no tolerance for any forms of abuse. As reported, one case was transferred to court this week in which a clergyman is accused of sexual crimes against minors. The priest from the Archdiocese of Vilnius is suspected of 34 instances of crimes relating to the sexual abuse of children, possession of pornographic material, and the involvement of children in alcohol consumption. There are 11 victims in the case, whose ages ranged from 12 to 18 years at the time when the crimes were allegedly committed. The media identified the suspect as priest Tadas Švedavičius, aged 56. The crimes might have been committed from 2002 to 2025. This case is related to another one, which was transferred to court at the end of June 2026. In the latter case, priest Ryšard Peciun from the Archdiocese of Vilnius, is suspected of possession of pornographic material depicting children. https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2026/.text: We’re kicking off with an exclusive interview with the EU’s climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, who told my colleague Maria Tadeo that Europe must invest more to protect itself from climate disasters, despite capitals’ tight budgets. More in our top story below.But first – Brussels awakens from its summer slumber this morning to a cold shower from the north: Iceland has voted 52.8% to 47.2% against restarting EU membership talks, freezing the possibility of joining the bloc for the foreseeable future.A chilly setback: It’s a major knock for Brussels, where officials have been pushing to reinvigorate the EU’s enlargement agenda in recent months. The ‘No’ from Icelanders raises major questions over the EU’s ability to attract wealthier, northern countries to its ranks, with all current candidates lagging severely behind Reykjavik on economic indicators.The response from the EU institutions has been notably muted – with a Commission spokesperson issuing a few brief words “taking note” of the result. European Council President António Costa exchanged messages with Iceland’s Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir on Sunday, saying the EU “fully respects the democratic choice of the Icelandic population” and vowing to continue strengthening the bilateral relationship.Meanwhile, hard-right leaders including Marine Le Pen took the opportunity to hail the outcome as a win for national sovereignty.Despite the temptation to frame the vote as a geopolitical reckoning – amid US threats against Greenland, Trump’s tariffs and China’s assertiveness – concerns over Iceland’s lucrative fishing industry ultimately proved decisive.The fish factor: Fish accounts for a massive 40% of Iceland’s export value, and Icelandic fishers land more fish annually than any other EU nation. Fish – as it did in the 2016 Brexit referendum – became a highly politicised symbol of Iceland’s sovereignty, with many industries warning against losing control over the country’s prized 760,000 square kilometre exclusive economic zone (EEZ).Taking ‘control’: Iceland’s powerful fishing industry had been spooked at the prospect of joining the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy (CFP), a set of rules for managing the EU fleet and conserving fish stocks, despite officials in Brussels saying they were open to “creative solutions” in talks on Iceland’s access to the bloc’s agriculture and fisheries programmes.Speaking to Europe Today earlier, Margrét Ágústa Sigurðardóttir, secretary general of the Icelandic Farmers Association, also said the desire to avoid joining the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) had been a crucial factor in the vote. “Icelanders voted to keep decisions about Iceland in Iceland,” she said, stressing that the island had not “rejected Europe”, but rather “full EU membership”.‘Very disappointed’: Pro-EU voices have meanwhile been left deflated by the narrow defeat. Former Reykjavik mayor Dagur B. Eggertsson told Europe Today that he was “disappointed” after what he described as a “very harsh campaign”, which he said had “echoes of Brexit and the Brexit playbook”.My colleague Jorge Liboreiro has these four takeaways from the referendum result, and Vincenzo Genovese has more on the implications for Brussels.NATO security under spotlight: How secure is the central military operational headquarters at the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), and who wants to spy on it? These questions are at the heart of a court case playing out in Mons, Belgium today. My colleague Angela Skujins writes in to report on the unravelling espionage tale from the usually quiet country town now sitting at the centre of a security scandal. In July, the Belgian Federal Prosecutor’s Office arrested a Canadian national of Chinese origin for allegedly carrying out spy activities for a third country while interning at NATO’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe. She was ordered to remain in detention before the trial kicked off — something her legal team has appealed.So, who is she? And was she spying for China? Investigative media Follow The Money reports that the individual is a woman in her thirties called Claire Biwei Zhang, and may have been abetted by accomplices while the Belgian authorities mounted their legal case. While a lot of this case is confidential, we do know that pre-trial detention underscores the veracity of the charges and what potentially is at stake, with media reports filling in the blanks. Angela will have more details from the Mons courthouse during the day.Also today: Hungary could meet all EU criteria to unlock €10 billion in post-Covid EU recovery funds as soon as today, my colleague Sándor Zsiros reports. To unlock the cash, frozen under the previous government of Viktor Orbán, Budapest needs to deliver on 27 so-called milestones, including judicial and anti-corruption reforms, by the end of today.Both Hungarian and EU officials have previously told Sándor that work is progressing well, and that it was “realistic” for Budapest to meet its targets on time. The government led by Prime Minister Péter Mayar has said it wants to “bring home every cent due to Hungary.”‘Europe’s climate and security challenges are inseparable,’ Commissioner Hoekstra tells EuronewsEurope must invest more to protect itself from increasingly severe climate disasters, EU Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra has exclusively told Euronews, warning that paying for the damage after fires and floods strike will cost the bloc far more.“All evidence shows that making the upfront investments is way cheaper than just being hit by fire, being hit by floods and then paying for the damage. That’s just way more costly,” Hoekstra told our EU Editor Maria Tadeo in an interview for Europe Today, Euronews' flagship morning show.Describing the summer as “dramatic”, the Dutch commissioner said the EU was better prepared than last year, with more firefighters, planes and helicopters deployed, but the scale of destruction had barely improved.An area twice the size of Luxembourg was lost to fires, while estimates of the economic damage range from €50 billion to €70 billion or more. Spain and France lost thousands of hectares to blazes, while at least 14 first responders died fighting the fires.Pressed by Euronews for a specific figure, Hoekstra did not commit to one but suggested the bulk of the funding would still come from national budgets.“We need to be crystal clear about who is responsible for what. What is for the local governments, what is for regional governments, what is for national governments and what is for Europe,” he said.Hoekstra also underlined the importance of the climate transition for the EU’s economic sovereignty, amid continued uncertainty around the transit of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz,“In the medium term, by far our best bet is to move to a completely different energy system and that is where the money should be going,” Hoekstra said.Watch the full interview.Four days under fire: Kyiv battered by relentless Russian drone attacksKyiv has endured four consecutive days of air-raid alerts, with Russia sending waves of drones towards the Ukrainian capital and surrounding region throughout the day and night, my colleague Sasha Vakulina reports.The latest attacks continued through Sunday, with drones approaching the capital for hours at a time and explosions and air-defence fire heard across the city throughout the morning and afternoon.Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had launched almost 1,500 drones of all types over the four days alone, around 800 of them jet-powered.Zelenskyy admitted the jet-powered drones were the most difficult to intercept and were currently being countered mainly by Ukrainian combat aircraft. Kyiv is working to secure additional interceptors to defend against them, he added.Sasha explains why jet-powered drones have become Russia’s new weapon of choice. The attacks come as Kyiv prepares for fresh contacts with Washington. Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Ukraine was preparing for “new communication” with US President Donald Trump’s envoys, with further details expected on Monday.More from our newsroomsFrench presidential race: De Villepin set to run, Faure enters socialist primary. With just under eight months to go until the French presidential election, political manoeuvring is in full swing. Both Conservative politician Dominique De Villepin and Socialist leader Olivier Faure have suggested they will enter the race, Olivier Tolachides reports.Major manhunt underway after woman killed in shooting at Swiss rave. Shots were fired early on Sunday at an event attended by around 3,500 people in Aarau, Switzerland, killing at least one person and injuring five others. Police have launched a large-scale operation. Sonja Issel has the details.Iran fires retaliatory attacks following US strikes on Larak island. The US attacks on Iran are the first in around a month as the Trump administration had shifted its war objective to inflict maximum economic pain on Tehran. Washington says the strikes were aimed at preventing Iranian forces from disrupting global shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Malek Fouda has more.We're also keeping an eye onEU defence ministers arrive in Wicklow, Ireland, for dinner later this evening ahead of a Foreign Affairs Council focused on defence issues on Tuesday.The Bled Strategic Forum kicks off in Slovenia. European Commissioner for the Mediterranean, Dubravka Šuica, participates.That's it for today. We'll be back tomorrow. Angela Skujins, Sasha Vakulina, Jorge Liboreiro, Vincenzo Genovese, Marta Pacheco and Sandor Zsiros contributed to this newsletter.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: The patient, whose identity was not disclosed, had been sent to DR Congo by a humanitarian organisation to help support the response to the outbreak. Photograph: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP View image in fullscreen The patient, whose identity was not disclosed, had been sent to DR Congo by a humanitarian organisation to help support the response to the outbreak. Photograph: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP Ebola British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK Patient is ⁠in ​stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist ‘high consequence’ infectious disease unit Supported by About this content Sarah Johnson Wed 4 Nov 2026 13.18 EST First published on Wed 4 Nov 2026 11.32 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed. “A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola ,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.” The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters. A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak. The Royal Free hospital in London has a high-level isolation unit for infectious diseases such as Ebola; other centres are in Newcastle and Liverpool. Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness . It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies. The current outbreak, declared on 15 May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases, and 5,000 deaths . It is the 17th in DR Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus, and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history. The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way . Since the outbreak started, it has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last month Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja , after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus. She, along with a close contact, were evacuated to Switzerland for treatment. In an interview with the Guardian last month, Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said the “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak meant it could reach the UK and other countries. “We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment. “It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented.” Other patients who have been medically evacuated for specialised care since the start of the outbreak include two sent to Germany and one to the Netherlands . Another case was reported in France in July . British health authorities say the risk ⁠to the wider public from imported Ebola cases remains low and the NHS has procedures in place to manage suspected and confirmed infections. There have only been four confirmed cases recorded in Britain since 1976, ‌according to the UK Health Security Agency. https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/17/beyo.text: For years, the business case for industrial decarbonization centred on a simple calculation: how much more would a “cleaner” technology cost, and how much would it reduce emissions? Today, that “green premium” remains important, but it is no longer the only consideration. Commercial priorities, geopolitical pressures and government policies increasingly shape investment decisions and the shift towards lower-carbon alternatives.A low-carbon product can cost more but still be the smarter business choiceAs a result, a low-carbon product can cost more but still be the smarter business choice. Companies investing in clean technologies must therefore weigh a broader set of factors, including volatile energy and material costs, value chain resilience, market opportunities and risks, government policies affecting industrial competitiveness, and their positioning in the low-carbon economy. In short, we are moving “beyond the green premium”.For heavy industry, decarbonization has evolved from a narrow focus on sustainability costs to a strategic decision about the products companies will make, the markets they will serve and the supply sources on which they can rely. This shift has emerged as a clear message from the First Movers Coalition’s work with hard-to-abate industries throughout 2026.To understand this broader calculation, it is worth revisiting the “green premium”, a term coined by Bill Gates in 2020 to describe “the difference in cost between a product that involves emitting carbon and an alternative that doesn’t”. The concept made the economics of decarbonization visible, but it never told the whole story.The cost of cutting emissions varies widely for technologies and projectsIn all sectors, the cost of cutting emissions varies widely for technologies and projects. For example, in cement production, emissions reductions of up to 50% can be achieved at negligible or low cost through clinker substitution and other supplementary routes, but further reductions often command a significant premium. By contrast, sustainable aviation fuels can cost at least twice their fossil fuel equivalent, with an even higher premium for more advanced technologies. Treating these different situations as one common economic problem obscures more than it clarifies.As companies look beyond the immediate price difference, three factors are reshaping how businesses assess the value of decarbonization: commercial realities, geopolitics and policy.In terms of commercial priorities, the cost of decarbonization is being assessed alongside competitiveness and growth rather than as a standalone sustainability cost. The green economy is already valued at more than $5 trillion (Editor's note: around €4.54 trillion) a year, and is expected to grow another $2 trillion (Editor's note: around €1.82 trillion) by 2030. For companies, this points to growing demand, new markets and the possibility of gaining an advantage by moving early.In stable conditions, fossil-based inputs may look cheaperThis does not mean that every low-carbon product will immediately compete on price. But focusing only on the green premium fails to ask who will be positioned to supply the market when demand grows, and who will have the capabilities and partnerships needed to respond.Geopolitics, conflict, supply-chain disruption and energy price shocks have exposed the risks of relying on a small number of energy sources and materials. In stable conditions, fossil-based inputs may look cheaper, but, depending on the sector, that advantage is quickly lost when supply is disrupted or prices spike.Jet fuel price spikes linked to conflict in the Middle East – topping $220/barrel in March (Editor's note: around 199 €) and $200/barrel (Editor's note: around 181 €) once more in September 2026 – illustrate how quickly the economics of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) can change.SAF remains more expensive, but the ongoing crisis has exposed what a simple price comparison leaves out: investment in SAF can reduce exposure to future energy shocks via diversified production. Early partnerships with producers can shorten and onshore supply chains, strengthening supply security and potentially lowering price volatility. For airlines, the question is not just what SAF costs, but what more resilient and diversified fuel supplies are worth.Government policy is reshaping the industrial landscapeFinally, government policy is reshaping the industrial landscape. Regulations, standards, subsidies, permitting rules and trade measures influence investment decisions, determining which products qualify for public support, which projects can be developed quickly, and which supply chains retain access to major markets.The EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) – which is currently being debated – illustrates this shift. Alongside industrial decarbonization, it explicitly seeks to reduce Europe’s reliance on external suppliers and increase the share of strategic manufacturing from 14.3% in 2024 to 20% by 2035. Meanwhile, the Net Zero Industry Act is already linking decarbonization strategies with streamlined permitting and faster environmental procedures.The green premium remains a useful starting point, but investment decisions demand a broader calculation: will the savings from postponing decarbonization will survive the next energy shock, supply disruption, or policy change?In this turbulent era, the cost of waiting – from lost market access and volatile input prices to weaker supply chains and missed investment opportunities – may ultimately be higher. As with any business case, there are risks, but the opportunities that decarbonization offers have never been greater.Noam Boussidan is the Head of the First Movers Coalition. He has 15+ years’ experience at the crossroads of climate, energy and industry transformation, having held various positions across government, private sector and non-governmental work. The First Movers Coalition (FMC) is the World Economic Forum’s flagship industry decarbonization initiative. A global coalition of companies leveraging their purchasing power to decarbonize the world's heavy-emitting industrial sectors responsible for 25% of global emissions. The FMC has 100+ members from top global corporations who have come together to send a demand signal for emerging climate technologies.

https://www.politico.eu/article/gabriel-.text: PARIS — Gabriel Zucman wants to put the world’s billionaires on notice. The 40-year-old French economist, who has spent more than a decade designing ways to tax the ultra-rich, hosts a summit against “international oligarchy” in Paris on Saturday. It comes less than three weeks after California voters rejected a billionaire tax he backed, in a campaign where Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other opponents spent more than $300 million to thwart the initiative. “Everywhere, we see very, very strong popular support for taxing billionaires,” Zucman told POLITICO this week, arguing that his loss in California was only a minor setback. “That’s true even in the United States.” Advertisement Advertisement Zucman sees fresh hope in the results of the U.S. midterms, in which a string of Democrats campaigning to tax the ultra-rich won their races. “Now our party has a choice to make: Are we going to stand with the working class or the tech lords?” said Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who is flying in for the Paris gathering. “The same inequality is fueling anger and distrust not only in America, but also in France and around the world,” he told POLITICO. Khanna and Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) are due to speak at the Théâtre de la Concorde, a city-owned venue off the Champs-Élysées loaned for the occasion by Emmanuel Grégoire, the socialist mayor of Paris. Left-wing leaders from Italy, Brazil, Spain and the U.K. are also expected to attend. A “Paris Manifesto” published Friday calls for a minimum tax on the largest fortunes, protections for independent media and rules for artificial intelligence. The question is whether anyone outside the theater will buy into Zucman’s ideas. His signature proposal, a minimum annual tax of 2% on the largest fortunes, was rejected by the French Senate last year. “It’s a real program to save our democracy,” said Eva Joly, a former French investigating judge who jailed the boss of oil giant Elf in the 1990s and later served as a European lawmaker for the Greens. Zucman “carries it brilliantly,” she told POLITICO. Advertisement Advertisement The fight goes on Global talks on taxing the super-rich have stalled this year under the U.S. presidency of the G20, according to Zucman, who expects the impasse to persist as long as Donald Trump is in the White House. Still, he hopes to revive the debate when Britain takes over the G20 presidency next year. In Brussels, meanwhile, tax legislation generally requires the unanimous agreement of all 27 EU governments, making a bloc-wide solution difficult. Rather than wait for international agreement, Zucman expects individual governments to take the lead, just as France did with value-added tax in the 1950s and several EU countries have done more recently with digital services taxes. Gabriel Zucman gives a press conference on the launch of the European Tax Observatory, on June 1, 2021 in Brussels. | Pool photo by François Walschaerts via AFP/Getty Images Bills to tax the wealthy are in the works in the Netherlands, Belgium and Spain, he said, while the British government has begun looking at the idea. Joly is less ready to write off Brussels, calling the EU “a field of possibilities.” She argued that low taxes on multinationals distort competition with domestic firms and said it was the responsibility of the European Commission and Parliament to address the problem. There are also signs of movement on corporate taxation. European Council President António Costa is weighing a tax on U.S. tech giants to help fund the EU’s next seven-year budget, POLITICO reported Thursday, after Trump’s poor showing in the midterms eased fears of retaliation by Washington. Advertisement Advertisement “Europe cannot afford to calibrate its tax policy to America’s mood swings,” said Paul Monaghan, chief executive of the U.K.-based Fair Tax Foundation, which campaigns on corporate tax conduct. At the United Nations, negotiators will meet in Nairobi from Nov. 30 to Dec. 10 for the next round of talks on a global tax convention, with a final text due in 2027. Beyond the left In California, Zucman said, billionaires flooded voters with “disinformation” that the tax would bankrupt the health system, even though 90% of the revenue raised would have gone toward health care. But money was only part of the story. Unions split over the measure, POLITICO reported, and Gov. Gavin Newsom campaigned against it . A state-only wealth tax “creates economic incentives for money and jobs to leave the state,” his chief of staff, Nathan Barankin, said. Zucman rejects the notion that Saturday’s gathering is a rally of the left. He said he had invited former EU competition chief Margrethe Vestager and former Italian Prime Minister Mario Draghi, but both declined. A spokesperson for Vestager declined to comment. Yet in France, the far-left France Unbowed party and the Greens were the only ones to fully embrace Zucman’s proposed 2% annual wealth tax ahead of next spring’s presidential election. MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, who is running for a left-wing coalition that includes the Socialists, has instead proposed to raise the tax rate for inheritances above €1.8 million, and a one-off 5% levy on fortunes over €100 million. Advertisement Advertisement François Geerolf, an economist at Sciences Po’s OFCE, has challenged Zucman’s arguments. In a paper updated last month , he argued that Zucman had exaggerated the extent to which billionaires are undertaxed and proposed a remedy that could do more harm than good. Geerolf acknowledged that the ultra-rich can use holding companies to shield income from taxation, but argued for closing the loophole instead of imposing an annual tax on fortunes. He also questioned estimates that the tax would raise €20 billion a year in France, putting the likely proceeds at just €2 billion to €6 billion. His verdict: “A real problem, a false diagnosis, a bad remedy.” Other critics have also been mobilizing. Trop c’est trop ("Enough is enough"), a campaign group backed by business executive Eric Maumy, presented a study Wednesday characterizing Zucman's tax proposal as confiscatory and unconstitutional. But Zucman believes it is the status quo that is untenable. “Do you think it’s normal that billionaires can pay zero personal tax?” he said. “It’s the current situation that is radical.”
